newsitem.title: USA: Clinton campaigns in Dole's Republican heartland.
newsitem.headline: Clinton campaigns in Dole's Republican heartland.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

Even though polls indicate his re-election is already in the bag, President Bill Clinton hit the campaign trail again on Sunday as Republican Bob Dole extended his stay in vote-rich California in a bid to revive his fortunes.

Clinton was scheduled to embark on a seven-state trip, starting with a rally in Virginia, one of several normally Republican southern states he had a reasonable chance of winning in the Nov. 5 election.
The Reuters daily tracking poll showed Clinton increasing his lead over Dole among likely voters to 13.4 percentage points. The CNN/USA Today Gallup poll showed Clinton leading by 20 points.
If that lead held until Election Day Clinton would be in position to score a landslide of historical proportions.
Republican pollster Robert Teeter said there was little reason for Dole to hope for a last-minute reverse in the final days of a campaign where Clinton's lead has stayed remarkably stable for months.
"There's no evidence that there's anything going on or changing. There's no dynamic in this election," he said.
The focus was turning to the battle for control of Congress, where Democrats were pushing to regain majorities two years after Republicans took control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

"Everything I see gives me optimism that we will win both houses back. The Republicans botched a wonderful opportunity they had two years ago. They were radical. They were extreme," said Rep. Richard Gephardt of Missouri, who would become House Speaker if the Democrats took over.
But Republicans maintained that polls showed them with a good chance of keeping control of both the Senate and the House.

Dole decided to stay an extra day in California, hoping to revive his challenge for the state's 54 Electoral College votes -- one fifth of the 270 needed to win the presidency in the U.S. indirect election system.
His California campaign manager Ken Khachigian told reporters Dole remained the underdog but maintained that the Republican was making headway among women voters.
"I'm looking for votes in every little nook and cranny," Khachigian said.

In recent days Dole's speeches turned increasingly sour and abrasive. He not only attacked the media but even the public for failing to pay attention to what Dole believed were Clinton's serious ethical shortcomings.
"How long do you think the American people are going to take it? Wake up, America. Wake up, America! Wake up, America!" Dole exhorted in a campaign rally in Fresno, California, on Saturday.
White House adviser George Stephanopoulos, interviewed on NBC's "Meet the Press," said Clinton and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton had done nothing wrong.
"Bob Dole ought to apologize" for some of the claims he has made in recent days, Stephanopoulos said.
Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, stuck in signle digits in the polls, maintained his own assault on Clinton's ethics in an interview on the same program.
"You should never let anyone be president of the United States who does not have a strong moral and ethical base," Perot said.

Dole's campaign manager Scott Reed said Dole was within striking distance in Ohio, Michigan and Missouri said. The base of the party in the South was coming back to Dole and he was optimistic about the Rocky Mountain states.
